claims.text: The starting composite contains discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments embedded in a Cu matrix.
The untreated W–Cu interface is prone to phase separation and interfacial void formation under service conditions.
W particles should be uniformly coated with a thin Ni layer before composite consolidation.
A thin Ni coating on W will improve bonding between W and the Cu matrix.
A thin Ni coating on W will suppress phase separation at the W–Cu interface.
A thin Ni coating on W will suppress interfacial void formation.
The Ni coating will form a metallurgically bonded interlayer at the W–Cu interface.
The Ni interlayer will improve wetting at the W–Cu interface.
Improved wetting will promote stronger interfacial bonding.
The Ni interlayer will produce controlled interdiffusion at the W–Cu interface.
Improved adhesion and reduced diffusional instability will mitigate void formation and microstructural inhomogeneity.
A more coherent W–Cu interface will facilitate electron and phonon transport.
The Ni-coated composite will have fewer interfacial voids and less phase separation than the untreated composite after thermal and irradiation exposure.
The Ni-coated composite will have higher effective thermal conductivity than the untreated composite under high-heat-flux and irradiation conditions.
Void formation and phase separation in untreated W–Cu degrade thermal conductivity.
The intervention is expected to be effective when manufacturing can reliably produce thin Ni coatings and service conditions represent W plasma-facing/Cu cooling-component interfaces.
The optimal Ni coating thickness and long-term stability under extreme irradiation are unresolved.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity enhancement and the long-term irradiation behavior are uncertain.
